title: Prime Factorization
short: Write a number as a product of primes with a factor tree.
trouble: Children stop at a composite factor like 4 and call the factor tree finished.

blocks.html: A prime number has exactly two factors, 1 and itself. Every other whole number greater than 1 is composite: it splits into smaller factors. Keep splitting, and you reach the primes that build the number.

To find the prime factorization, split the number into two factors, then split any factor that is not prime. Stop only when every branch ends in a prime. Then write the number as the product of those primes.

Each split makes the factors smaller, so the splitting has to stop, and it can only stop at primes. However you begin, you end with the same primes: $60 = 6 \times 10$ and $60 = 4 \times 15$ both lead to $2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 5$.

blocks.cap: A factor tree for 60, started as $6 \times 10$. Split the numbers that are not prime. Then press “Start over” and try a different first split: the primes at the ends come out the same.

blocks.title: Peel off small primes
blocks.q: Write 126 as a product of primes.
steps: 63 is not even, but $6 + 3 = 9$, so 3 divides it: $63 = 3 \times 21$.

blocks.html: Stopping at a composite factor, like writing $60 = 2 \times 2 \times 15$. The number 15 is not prime ($15 = 3 \times 5$), so the tree is not finished. Check each factor: can it be divided by 2, 3, 5 or 7 without leaving a remainder? If so, split it.
You can write repeated primes with an exponent, like $2^{2} \times 3 \times 5$. You will meet exponents properly with powers of ten.
